newsitem.title: USA: IMF sees strong Finnish growth, worried at jobless.
newsitem.headline: IMF sees strong Finnish growth, worried at jobless.

text.p: The Finnish economy will grow strongly this year but comprehensive structural reforms are needed to reduce a stubbornly high unemployment rate, the International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday.
A statement issued after the IMF's annual review of the Finnish economy said inflation could rise slightly in 1997, but it would remain below the government's two percent target.
It said the government had little scope for tax cuts in 1998, unless these were matched with spending cuts. Tighter fiscal policy might be needed if inflation picked up sharply.

"The favorable outlook is expected to continue in 1997," the IMF said. "Growth of output is projected to be robust, supported by both domestic and external demand ... External balances will remain strong."
The IMF forecast 4.7 percent growth in gross domestic product in 1997, up from 3.3 percent in 1996. It expected consumer price inflation to rise to 1.3 percent, from 0.6 percent last year.
But the IMF said unemployment would only decline to 14.8 percent, from 16.3 percent in 1996.

"Directors noted that unemployment remained high and reducing it remained a priority, requiring not only a continuation of cautious macroeconomic policies, but also comprehensive structural reforms," the statement said.

The IMF reviews the economy of each of its member states each year and frequently issues a press release summarizing its conclusions. The IMF said its board had assessed the Finnish economy on July 14.
The IMF welcomed Finland's plans to keep spending tight in 1998 but said public finances should be consolidated further.
"Directors generally thought that there was little scope to cut taxes in 1998 unless those cuts were matched with expenditure cuts," it said.

"Indeed signs of a possible pickup in inflation, such as the rapid increase in some asset prices, could warrant a tightening of policies. That would need to come in good measure from fiscal policy, given the more limited degree of monetary independence arising from Finland's ERM participation," it said.
The IMF also welcomed Finland's decision to join Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism and said the rate at which the markka entered the system was "broadly in line with macroeconomic fundamentals".
